subject: Genetic Distance between populations with HLA genotypes

messages.author: f8b7b1c5a69c9952
messages.subject: Genetic Distance between populations with HLA genotypes
parts:
Hi Zhian,

I'm wondering how to structure my data for calculating genetic distance between multiple populations of patient samples, where each patient within each population has an HLA genotype.  Here, I am interested in modeling the distances between HLA class I genotypes (HLA class I is comprised of HLA A, B, and C).  The class I genes are multi-allelic; though each gene has two alleles. I.e. for one patient, the genotype might be: A0201,A3101,B3502,B3906,C0702,C0401, where  A0201 & A3101 are the alleles at HLA A, etc. 

I've been studying this page- https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/Pop_Structure.html and https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/Data_Preparation.html to try to learn how to structure the input data to make a genclone object, but I'm still confused.  How can the alleles be encoded for each gene and for each patient?  I would really appreciate any tips you might have.  Thank you!

Best,
Chirag

messages.author: d192ec4b1d416345
messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Genetic Distance between populations with HLA genotypes
parts:
Hi,

As these are co-dominant loci, you can code them as you would diploid microsatellite data (e.g. https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/Data_Preparation.html#diploids).
You don't have to code your data like that if you have it in a different format. If you can get your data in a single data frame with one column per locus, then you can import it with adegenet. See section 4 of the adegenet tutorial: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/blob/master/tutorials/tutorial-basics.pdf

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Thanks!  This is very helpful- I think I'm close.  However, it seems that in genind objects there is a field called @loc.n.all, which stores the number of alleles per locus.  The adegenet manual says that the range of alleles per locus is 8-18, but there are many more than 18 alleles for each HLA gene (e.g. greater than 30 alleles for each of HLA-A, B, and C) present in my data.  Is there a way to get around this?  Thanks again!

Best,
Chirag
